board_events.latex: \vec L = \vec r \times \vec p = \vec r \times m\vec v

board_events.text: First term: $\vec v \times m\vec v = \vec 0$, since a vector is parallel to itself.
Conservation of angular momentum falls straight out as a corollary.

segments.text: This is the derivation C B S E asks for most: proving that the rate of change of angular momentum equals the applied torque. From it, conservation of angular momentum falls out instantly.
Keep the figure in mind. A particle has position r and momentum p, and its angular momentum L points out of the plane. The key move is that one term will vanish.
Step one, start from the definition. The angular momentum of a particle is r cross p, which is r cross m v.

Step two, differentiate both sides with respect to time. Since a cross product has two factors that both change, apply the product rule, carefully keeping the order: it is dee r by dee t cross p, plus r cross dee p by dee t.

Step three, look at that first term and watch it vanish. Dee r by dee t is the velocity v, and p is m v, so the term is v cross m v. A vector crossed with itself is zero, because v is parallel to itself. Velocity and momentum point the same way, so they contribute no turning.
Step four, the second term. By Newton second law, dee p by dee t is the force F. So the rate of change of angular momentum is r cross F, which is exactly the torque.
Step five is the result: the net external torque equals the rate of change of angular momentum. This is Newton second law written in angular language.

<excited> And the corollary is immediate. If the net external torque is zero, the rate of change of L is zero, so L stays constant. That single line is the conservation of angular momentum, and the dancer, the coupling wheels, and the orbiting planet all obey it.
यह वह derivation है जो C B S E सबसे ज़्यादा माँगता है — यह prove करना कि angular momentum के change की rate applied torque के बराबर है। इससे conservation of angular momentum तुरंत निकल आता है।
Figure याद रखिए। एक particle की position r और momentum p है, और उसका angular momentum L plane से बाहर point करता है। असली चाल यह है कि एक term ग़ायब हो जाएगा।
Step one — definition से शुरू करो। किसी particle का angular momentum है r cross p, जो r cross m v है।

Step two — दोनों तरफ़ time के respect में differentiate करो। Cross product के दोनों factors बदलते हैं, इसलिए product rule लगाओ, order ध्यान से रखते हुए — यह है dee r by dee t cross p, plus r cross dee p by dee t।

Step three — उस पहले term को देखो और ग़ायब होते देखो। Dee r by dee t है velocity v, और p है m v, तो term है v cross m v। कोई vector खुद से cross करने पर zero है, क्योंकि v खुद के parallel है। Velocity और momentum एक ही दिशा में हैं, तो कोई turning नहीं देते।
Step four — दूसरा term। Newton के second law से, dee p by dee t है force F। तो angular momentum के change की rate है r cross F, जो ठीक torque है।
Step five result है — net external torque बराबर angular momentum के change की rate। यह angular भाषा में लिखा Newton का second law है।

<excited> और corollary तुरंत है। अगर net external torque zero है, तो L के change की rate zero है, यानी L constant रहता है। वही एक line conservation of angular momentum है, और dancer, coupling wheels तथा orbiting planet, सब इसे मानते हैं।

board_events.latex: \vec\tau = \vec r \times \vec F = \begin{vmatrix}\hat i & \hat j & \hat k\\ x & y & z\\ F_x & F_y & F_z\end{vmatrix}

board_events.text: For planar problems only the k-term survives: positive is anticlockwise, negative is clockwise.
Take $\vec r = 2\hat i + 3\hat j$ metres and $\vec F = 5\hat i + \hat j$ newtons.
The negative sign says the force tends to rotate the body clockwise about the origin.
The same machinery, with $\vec p = m\vec v$ in the bottom row, gives angular momentum.

segments.text: When you are handed vectors directly, the determinant is the fastest route to torque, and to angular momentum with one small change.
The figure shows a planar case. Position r and force F lie in the plane, and the torque points out of it, its sign telling you the sense of rotation.
Write r in the middle row and F in the bottom row of the determinant, with i, j, k across the top, then expand as usual.
For a two-dimensional, planar problem only the k-term survives. A positive k means anticlockwise, a negative k means clockwise; the sign hands you the direction for free.
Take a quick illustration: r is two i plus three j metres, and F is five i plus j newtons.
The k-component is x times F-y minus y times F-x. That is two times one minus three times five, which is two minus fifteen, so minus thirteen newton metres.

<whisper> The negative sign tells you the force tends to rotate the body clockwise about the origin. You never had to draw an angle or find a perpendicular distance; the determinant handled the geometry and the sign in one shot.
And the very same machinery, with momentum m v in the bottom row instead of force, gives you the angular momentum. One method, two quantities.
जब vectors सीधे दिए हों, तो determinant torque तक का सबसे तेज़ रास्ता है, और एक छोटे से बदलाव से angular momentum तक भी।
Figure एक planar case दिखाती है। Position r और force F plane में हैं, और torque उससे बाहर point करता है, उसका sign rotation का sense बताता है।
Determinant की middle row में r और bottom row में F लिखो, ऊपर i, j, k, फिर हमेशा की तरह expand करो।
एक two-dimensional, planar problem के लिए सिर्फ़ k-term बचता है। Positive k मतलब anticlockwise, negative k मतलब clockwise; sign direction मुफ़्त में दे देता है।
एक झटपट illustration लो — r है two i plus three j metres, और F है five i plus j newtons।
k-component है x गुणा F-y minus y गुणा F-x। यानी two गुणा one minus three गुणा five, जो two minus fifteen, तो minus thirteen newton metres।

<whisper> Negative sign बताता है कि force body को origin के बारे में clockwise घुमाने की कोशिश करता है। आपको न angle खींचना पड़ा, न perpendicular distance निकालनी; determinant ने geometry और sign एक ही झटके में सँभाल लिए।
और वही machinery, bottom row में force की जगह momentum m v रखकर, आपको angular momentum देती है। एक method, दो quantities।

board_events.text: Given: $F = 40$ N, $r = 0.25$ m, $\theta = 30^\circ$.
Carry the unit newton metre, never joules; state the sense if asked.
Answer: the torque is 5 N m.
Only the perpendicular component, through the sine, does the turning.

segments.text: A clean board-level torque calculation. A mechanic applies a force of forty newtons at the end of a spanner a quarter of a metre long, and the force makes a thirty-degree angle with the handle. Find the torque about the bolt.
The figure sets it up: the bolt at the pivot, the spanner as the position vector, and the force pulling off at thirty degrees to the handle.
Write the givens: the force is forty newtons, the length is zero point two five metres, and the angle is thirty degrees.
Apply the torque formula: torque equals r times F times sine theta.
Substitute: zero point two five times forty times sine thirty degrees. Sine thirty is one half, so it is zero point two five times forty times one half, which equals five newton metres.
A presentation note that earns marks: always carry the unit newton metre, never joules, and state the sense of rotation if the question asks.
So the torque is five newton metres.
And notice why the sine appears: only the component of the force perpendicular to the spanner does the turning, and sine theta picks out exactly that component.

एक साफ़ board-level torque calculation। एक mechanic एक चौथाई metre लंबे spanner के सिरे पर forty newtons का force लगाता है, और force handle के साथ thirty-degree का angle बनाता है। Bolt के बारे में torque निकालो।
Figure इसे set करती है — pivot पर bolt, position vector के रूप में spanner, और handle से thirty degrees पर खिंचता force।
Givens लिखो — force forty newtons, length zero point two five metres, और angle thirty degrees।
Torque formula लगाओ — torque बराबर r गुणा F गुणा sine theta।
Substitute करो — zero point two five गुणा forty गुणा sine thirty degrees। Sine thirty है one half, तो यह zero point two five गुणा forty गुणा one half, जो बराबर five newton metres।
एक presentation note जो marks दिलाती है — हमेशा unit newton metre रखो, कभी joules नहीं, और अगर question माँगे तो rotation का sense बताओ।
तो torque है five newton metres।
और ध्यान दो sine क्यों आता है — force का सिर्फ़ वह component जो spanner के perpendicular है, turning करता है, और sine theta ठीक वही component चुन लेता है।

board_events.caption: I to two fifths I; omega to two point five omega

board_events.text: Trap: kinetic energy is not conserved; the muscles do work, so it rises.
She reduces her moment of inertia to $\tfrac{2I}{5}$; conserve $L = I\omega$.
Using $K = \tfrac{L^2}{2I}$ with $L$ fixed, kinetic energy scales as $1/I$.
So both the spin and the energy rise by a factor of two point five.

segments.text: A N E E T speed trap that catches students on energy. A dancer with arms out has moment of inertia I and angular speed omega. She pulls her arms in, reducing the moment of inertia to two fifths of I. Find her new angular speed and the ratio of new to old rotational kinetic energy.
The figure shows the trade. The moment of inertia drops to two fifths, and the angular speed rises to keep the product fixed.

Here is the trap. Students assume kinetic energy is conserved, as in a collision. It is not. The dancer muscles do work pulling the arms in, so the kinetic energy increases. Only angular momentum is conserved.
So conserve angular momentum, the moment of inertia times omega. The new moment of inertia is two fifths of I.
Set the products equal: I omega equals two fifths I times the new omega. The I cancels, giving the new omega as five halves of omega, that is two point five omega.

For the energy, use kinetic energy equals L squared over two I, with L held fixed. Then kinetic energy scales as one over the moment of inertia, so the ratio of new to old is I over two fifths I, which is five halves, or two point five.
In words, because angular momentum is fixed, the kinetic energy is inversely proportional to the moment of inertia.

<chuckle> So both the spin rate and the rotational kinetic energy rise by a factor of two point five. She spins faster and has more energy, exactly what your intuition says when someone powers up a spin. The extra energy came from her muscles, not from nowhere.

एक N E E T speed trap जो students को energy पर फँसाता है। बाहें फैलाए एक dancer का moment of inertia I और angular speed omega है। वह बाहें अंदर खींचती है, moment of inertia को I के two fifths तक घटाते हुए। उसकी नई angular speed और नई-से-पुरानी rotational kinetic energy का ratio निकालो।
Figure trade दिखाती है। Moment of inertia two fifths तक गिरता है, और angular speed ऊपर उठती है ताकि product fixed रहे।

यहाँ trap है। Students मान लेते हैं कि kinetic energy conserved है, जैसे किसी collision में। नहीं है। Dancer की muscles बाहें खींचते हुए work करती हैं, तो kinetic energy बढ़ती है। सिर्फ़ angular momentum conserved है।
तो angular momentum, यानी moment of inertia गुणा omega, conserve करो। नया moment of inertia I का two fifths है।
Products बराबर रखो — I omega बराबर two fifths I गुणा नया omega। I cancel, नया omega मिलता है omega का five halves, यानी two point five omega।

Energy के लिए kinetic energy बराबर L square बटा two I use करो, L fixed रखते हुए। तब kinetic energy moment of inertia के one over के proportional है, तो नई-से-पुरानी का ratio है I बटा two fifths I, जो five halves, यानी two point five।
शब्दों में — क्योंकि angular momentum fixed है, kinetic energy moment of inertia के inversely proportional है।

<chuckle> तो spin rate और rotational kinetic energy, दोनों two point five गुना बढ़ते हैं। वह तेज़ घूमती है और ज़्यादा energy रखती है, ठीक वही जो आपकी intuition कहती है जब कोई spin को powers up करता है। वह extra energy उसकी muscles से आई, कहीं से नहीं।

board_events.text: A particle of mass $m$ is launched at speed $u$, angle $\theta$; find $L$ about the launch point at the top.
At the top the horizontal velocity is perpendicular to the height $H$.
You needed projectile kinematics first, then the angular-momentum definition.

segments.text: A J E E Main problem that blends two topics. A particle of mass m is projected from the ground with speed u at angle theta. Find the magnitude of its angular momentum about the launch point when it reaches the highest point.
The figure shows the key instant. At the very top of the arc the velocity is purely horizontal, equal to u cosine theta, and the particle sits at the maximum height H directly above the launch point.
So this problem needs two ideas: first projectile kinematics to find the position and velocity at the top, then the angular-momentum definition.
From projectile motion, the maximum height is u squared sine squared theta over two g, and at the top the velocity is purely horizontal, u cosine theta, since the vertical component is zero there.

Now for angular momentum about the launch point, angular momentum is mass times the velocity times the perpendicular distance. At the top the horizontal velocity is exactly perpendicular to the vertical height H.
So L is m times u cosine theta times H. Substitute the height in place of H.
Tidy it up and the angular momentum is m u cubed sine squared theta cosine theta, all over two g, directed into the plane.

<curious> The lesson: you could not touch this without first extracting the height and the horizontal speed from kinematics, then applying the definition. That two-step blend is the signature of a J E E Main question.

एक J E E Main problem जो दो topics मिलाती है। Mass m का एक particle ground से speed u, angle theta पर project होता है। Highest point पर पहुँचने पर launch point के बारे में उसके angular momentum की magnitude निकालो।
Figure अहम instant दिखाती है। Arc के बिलकुल top पर velocity पूरी तरह horizontal है, u cosine theta के बराबर, और particle maximum height H पर launch point के ठीक ऊपर बैठा है।
तो इस problem को दो ideas चाहिए — पहले projectile kinematics से top पर position और velocity, फिर angular-momentum की definition।
Projectile motion से maximum height है u square sine square theta बटा two g, और top पर velocity पूरी तरह horizontal, u cosine theta, क्योंकि vertical component वहाँ zero है।
अब launch point के बारे में angular momentum के लिए — angular momentum है mass गुणा velocity गुणा perpendicular distance। Top पर horizontal velocity ठीक vertical height H के perpendicular है।
तो L है m गुणा u cosine theta गुणा H। H की जगह height substitute करो।
इसे साफ़ करो तो angular momentum है m u cube sine square theta cosine theta, बटा two g, plane के अंदर की ओर।
<curious> सबक़ — इसे आप छू भी नहीं सकते थे बिना पहले kinematics से height और horizontal speed निकाले, फिर definition लगाए। वही दो-step blend एक J E E Main question की पहचान है।

board_events.text: Rod mass $M$, length $L$, pivoted at one end; bullet $m$ at speed $v$ strikes and embeds at the free end.
The pivot force is impulsive but has zero torque about the pivot, so $L$ about the pivot is conserved.
Kinetic energy is not conserved here, which is why we used angular momentum, not energy.

segments.text: A J E E Advanced collision with rotation. A uniform rod of mass M and length L is pivoted at one end on a frictionless table, at rest. A bullet of mass m moving at speed v, perpendicular to the rod, strikes the free end and embeds. Find the angular speed of the rod-plus-bullet just after impact.

The figure holds the whole insight. During the collision the pivot exerts a large unknown impulsive force, so linear momentum is not conserved. But that pivot force acts at the pivot, so it has zero moment arm and zero torque about the pivot.
Write the setup: rod mass M, length L, pivoted at one end; bullet mass m at speed v striking the free end perpendicular to the rod.

So the right conserved quantity is angular momentum about the pivot. Because the collision is instantaneous and the pivot force has no torque there, that angular momentum is conserved through the impact. Choosing this axis is the whole trick.
Before impact only the bullet moves, and its angular momentum about the pivot is m v times L, the full length.

After impact, the moment of inertia is the rod about its end, M L squared over three, plus the embedded bullet as a point mass at distance L, that is m L squared. Set the before angular momentum equal to this moment of inertia times omega.
Solve for omega. It comes out to three m v over L times the quantity M plus three m.

<curious> Notice we never used energy. Kinetic energy is not conserved in this perfectly inelastic embedding, which is exactly why we leaned on angular momentum instead. Whenever a collision sticks, reach for the conserved quantity, not energy.

एक J E E Advanced collision जिसमें rotation है। Mass M, length L की एक uniform rod एक सिरे पर frictionless table पर pivoted है, at rest। Mass m की एक bullet, speed v से, rod के perpendicular, free end पर टकराकर धँस जाती है। Impact के ठीक बाद rod-plus-bullet की angular speed निकालो।

Figure में पूरी insight है। Collision के दौरान pivot एक बड़ा unknown impulsive force लगाता है, तो linear momentum conserved नहीं है। पर वह pivot force pivot पर ही act करता है, इसलिए उसका moment arm zero और pivot के बारे में torque zero है।
Setup लिखो — rod mass M, length L, एक सिरे पर pivoted; bullet mass m, speed v, free end पर rod के perpendicular टकराती।

तो सही conserved quantity है pivot के बारे में angular momentum। चूँकि collision instantaneous है और pivot force का वहाँ torque नहीं, वह angular momentum impact भर conserved रहता है। यही axis चुनना पूरी trick है।
Impact से पहले सिर्फ़ bullet चलती है, और pivot के बारे में उसका angular momentum है m v गुणा L, पूरी length।

Impact के बाद, moment of inertia है rod अपने end के बारे में, M L square बटा three, plus धँसी bullet एक point mass के रूप में distance L पर, यानी m L square। पहले वाले angular momentum को इस moment of inertia गुणा omega के बराबर रखो।
omega के लिए हल करो। यह निकलता है three m v बटा L गुणा quantity M plus three m।

<curious> ध्यान दो हमने energy इस्तेमाल ही नहीं की। इस perfectly inelastic embedding में kinetic energy conserved नहीं है, इसीलिए हमने angular momentum पर भरोसा किया। जब भी collision चिपके, conserved quantity की ओर जाओ, energy की नहीं।

sections.title: Common pitfalls and pro-tips

board_events.text: Torque and angular-momentum traps
1. Forgetting to specify the reference point; torque and $L$ are meaningless without it.
The same force gives different torques about different points; anchor your reference first.
2. Assuming energy is conserved when only angular momentum is, as in skater spins and inelastic hits.
3. Using the full force instead of its perpendicular component; only $F\sin\theta$ turns the body.
4. Writing torque in joules; it is a vector in newton metres, distinct from scalar energy.
Pro-tip: in collision-and-rotation problems, take $L$ about the pivot; the impulsive reaction drops out.
That single choice turns a messy two-unknown problem into a one-line conservation statement.

segments.text: Let us close torque and angular momentum with the four traps and the one pro-tip that saves entire questions.
Trap one: forgetting to specify the reference point. Torque and angular momentum are simply meaningless without answering about which point or axis.
The same force gives different torques about different points, so anchor your reference first and never switch it mid-solution.

Trap two: assuming energy is conserved when only angular momentum is. In skater spins, wheel-coupling, and inelastic rotational collisions, angular momentum survives but kinetic energy does not. Reach for energy conservation only when the process is genuinely lossless.

Trap three: using the full force instead of its perpendicular component. Only F sine theta, or equivalently the perpendicular distance times F, actually turns the body. The radial part is dead weight for rotation.

Trap four: writing torque in joules. Both torque and energy come out with newton-metre dimensions, but torque is a vector reported in newton metres, while energy is a scalar in joules. Keep them mentally separate.

<whisper> And the pro-tip that ties it together: in any collision-and-rotation problem, bullet in a rod, person jumping onto a turntable, always take angular momentum about the pivot or hinge. The unknown impulsive reaction there has zero moment arm, so it drops out automatically.
That single choice turns a messy two-unknown problem into a clean one-line conservation statement. It is the fastest tool in the whole subtopic.
Torque और angular momentum को उन चार traps और उस एक pro-tip के साथ बंद करते हैं जो पूरे questions बचाता है।
Trap one — reference point बताना भूल जाना। Torque और angular momentum, यह बताए बिना कि किस point या axis के बारे में, बस बेमानी हैं।
वही force अलग points के बारे में अलग torques देता है, इसलिए पहले अपना reference anchor करो और solution के बीच में उसे कभी मत बदलो।

Trap two — यह मानना कि energy conserved है जबकि सिर्फ़ angular momentum है। Skater spins, wheel-coupling और inelastic rotational collisions में angular momentum बचता है पर kinetic energy नहीं। Energy conservation की ओर तभी जाओ जब process सचमुच lossless हो।

Trap three — full force इस्तेमाल करना, उसके perpendicular component की जगह। सिर्फ़ F sine theta, या उसी तरह perpendicular distance गुणा F, body को turn करता है। Radial हिस्सा rotation के लिए dead weight है।

Trap four — torque को joules में लिखना। Torque और energy, दोनों की dimensions newton-metre हैं, पर torque एक vector है जो newton metres में बताया जाता है, जबकि energy एक scalar है joules में। इन्हें मन में अलग रखो।

<whisper> और वह pro-tip जो सब जोड़ता है — किसी भी collision-and-rotation problem में, rod में bullet, turntable पर कूदता व्यक्ति, हमेशा pivot या hinge के बारे में angular momentum लो। वहाँ का unknown impulsive reaction zero moment arm रखता है, तो अपने आप निकल जाता है।
वही एक choice एक messy two-unknown problem को एक साफ़ one-line conservation statement में बदल देती है। यह पूरे subtopic का सबसे तेज़ tool है।

board_events.text: A point particle only had to worry about one thing: the forces on it had to cancel.
A rigid body has size, so it can rotate even when the forces cancel.
Translational equilibrium: net force is zero, so the centre of mass does not accelerate.
Rotational equilibrium: net torque is zero, so the body does not start spinning.
Forces balanced but torques not: it spins. Torques balanced but forces not: it slides.
Only when both vanish is the body truly at rest and content to stay there.

segments.text: So far this chapter has been about making things move and spin. This subtopic asks the opposite question: when does a rigid body stay perfectly still, neither sliding away nor toppling over? That state is called equilibrium.

The figure shows why size changes everything. Push the top of a cupboard forward while a friend pushes the bottom backward with an equal force. The total force is zero, so it will not slide, yet it happily topples.
A point particle only ever had one thing to worry about to stay put: the forces on it had to cancel. That was the whole story.
But a rigid body has size, so it can do something a particle never could; it can rotate even when the forces cancel. Those two equal pushes create a turning effect.
So a rigid body needs two separate conditions. The first is translational equilibrium: the net force is zero, so the centre of mass does not accelerate and the body will not drift in any direction.
The second is rotational equilibrium: the net torque is zero, so the body does not start spinning. It will not topple or twist.
Both must hold. Forces balanced but torques unbalanced, and it spins. Torques balanced but forces unbalanced, and it slides.
<curious> Only when both the net force and the net torque vanish is the body truly at rest and content to stay there. This one idea powers every bridge, every shelf bracket, and every seesaw.
अब तक यह chapter चीज़ों को हिलाने और घुमाने के बारे में था। यह subtopic उलटा सवाल पूछता है — कोई rigid body बिलकुल स्थिर कब रहती है, न सरकती न गिरती? उस अवस्था को equilibrium कहते हैं।

Figure दिखाती है कि size सब कुछ क्यों बदल देता है। एक cupboard के top को आगे push करो जबकि एक दोस्त bottom को बराबर force से पीछे push करे। Total force zero है, तो वह सरकेगा नहीं, फिर भी ख़ुशी-ख़ुशी गिर जाता है।
एक point particle को स्थिर रहने के लिए बस एक चीज़ की चिंता थी — उस पर लगे forces cancel हो जाएँ। बस यही पूरी कहानी थी।
पर rigid body का size है, तो वह कुछ ऐसा कर सकती है जो particle कभी नहीं कर सकता; forces cancel होने पर भी घूम सकती है। वे दो बराबर pushes एक turning effect बनाते हैं।
तो rigid body को दो अलग conditions चाहिए। पहली है translational equilibrium — net force zero, तो centre of mass accelerate नहीं करता और body किसी दिशा में drift नहीं करती।
दूसरी है rotational equilibrium — net torque zero, तो body spin करना शुरू नहीं करती। वह न गिरेगी, न मुड़ेगी।
दोनों का होना ज़रूरी है। Forces balanced पर torques नहीं, तो घूमेगी। Torques balanced पर forces नहीं, तो सरकेगी।
<curious> सिर्फ़ तब जब net force और net torque, दोनों ग़ायब हों, body सचमुच at rest होती है और वहीं टिकी रहती है। यही एक idea हर bridge, हर shelf bracket, और हर seesaw को चलाता है।

board_events.text: Principle of moments: total clockwise moment equals total anticlockwise moment.
A heavy uncle near the pivot balances a small child far out: equal moments, not equal weights.
A lever multiplies a small effort into a large load; the factor is the mechanical advantage.
Centre of gravity: the single point where the whole weight effectively acts.
Support a body under its CG and it balances; anywhere else, gravity makes a toppling torque.
For everyday objects in uniform gravity, the CG sits exactly at the centre of mass.

segments.text: <curious> Closely tied to equilibrium is the everyday physics of balance, and it runs on one beautiful principle.
The figure shows a seesaw. A heavy uncle can sit near the pivot and still balance a small child sitting far out at the end.
That is the principle of moments: for balance, the total clockwise turning effect equals the total anticlockwise turning effect. Balance is about equal moments, not equal weights.
The child small weight times a big distance equals the uncle big weight times a small distance. Weight times distance from the pivot, matched on both sides.

This single principle powers every lever you have used, a crowbar, scissors, a bottle opener, even your own forearm. A lever lets a small effort move a large load by giving the effort a longer arm, and the factor by which it multiplies your force is the mechanical advantage.
Closely tied to balance is the centre of gravity, the single point where the body entire weight effectively acts.
Support a body exactly under its centre of gravity and it balances. Support it anywhere else and gravity produces a toppling torque about your support point.

And a link back to the last subtopic: for ordinary objects in uniform gravity, the centre of gravity sits exactly at the centre of mass. They only part company when gravity varies across a very tall body.
<curious> Equilibrium से गहराई से जुड़ी है balance की रोज़मर्रा physics, और यह एक सुंदर principle पर चलती है।
Figure एक seesaw दिखाती है। एक भारी uncle pivot के पास बैठकर भी सिरे पर दूर बैठे एक छोटे बच्चे को balance कर सकता है।
यही principle of moments है — balance के लिए total clockwise turning effect बराबर total anticlockwise turning effect। Balance बराबर moments की बात है, बराबर weights की नहीं।
बच्चे का छोटा weight गुणा बड़ी distance, uncle के बड़े weight गुणा छोटी distance के बराबर। Weight गुणा pivot से distance, दोनों तरफ़ मेल खाते।

यही एक principle हर lever को चलाता है जो आपने इस्तेमाल किया, crowbar, कैंची, bottle opener, यहाँ तक कि आपकी अपनी forearm। Lever एक छोटे effort को बड़ा load हिलाने देता है, effort को लंबा arm देकर, और जिस factor से यह आपका force बढ़ाता है वह mechanical advantage है।
Balance से गहराई से जुड़ा है centre of gravity, वह single point जहाँ body का पूरा weight असरदार तरीके से act करता है।
किसी body को ठीक उसके centre of gravity के नीचे support करो तो वह balance करती है। कहीं और support करो तो gravity आपके support point के बारे में एक toppling torque बनाती है।
और पिछले subtopic से एक कड़ी — uniform gravity में साधारण objects के लिए centre of gravity ठीक centre of mass पर बैठता है। वे तभी अलग होते हैं जब बहुत ऊँची body में gravity बदलती है।

board_events.text: Stable: CG rises on disturbance. Unstable: CG falls. Neutral: CG stays level.

segments.text: Here is the complete equilibrium toolkit. Two vector conditions, one balance rule, and the physics of levers and centre of gravity.
The figure adds the three types of equilibrium. A ball in a valley is stable, a ball on a hilltop is unstable, and a ball on a flat floor is neutral.

The first master condition is translational equilibrium: the sum of all external forces is the zero vector. In two dimensions this becomes the sum of the horizontal forces zero and the sum of the vertical forces zero.
The second is rotational equilibrium: the sum of all external torques is the zero vector. So the sum of torques about your chosen point must be zero.
For a simple lever, these collapse to the principle of moments: force one times distance one equals force two times distance two, the anticlockwise moment equal to the clockwise moment.
A lever mechanical advantage is the load over the effort, which equals the effort arm over the load arm. A long effort arm lets a small effort lift a big load.

A couple has torque equal to the force times the perpendicular distance between the two forces. And the centre of gravity is the weight-weighted average position, which equals the centre of mass when gravity is uniform.
Finally the three types of equilibrium, judged by how the centre of gravity moves on a small disturbance: it rises for stable, falls for unstable, and stays level for neutral.
यह रहा पूरा equilibrium toolkit। दो vector conditions, एक balance rule, और levers तथा centre of gravity की physics।
Figure तीन types of equilibrium जोड़ती है। घाटी में गेंद stable, पहाड़ी की चोटी पर गेंद unstable, और सपाट फ़र्श पर गेंद neutral।
पहली master condition है translational equilibrium — सारे external forces का sum zero vector। Two dimensions में यह बनता है horizontal forces का sum zero और vertical forces का sum zero।
दूसरी है rotational equilibrium — सारे external torques का sum zero vector। तो आपके चुने point के बारे में torques का sum zero होना चाहिए।
एक सादे lever के लिए ये principle of moments में सिमट जाती हैं — force one गुणा distance one बराबर force two गुणा distance two, anticlockwise moment बराबर clockwise moment।
Lever की mechanical advantage है load बटा effort, जो बराबर है effort arm बटा load arm। लंबा effort arm एक छोटे effort को बड़ा load उठाने देता है।
एक couple का torque बराबर है force गुणा दोनों forces के बीच की perpendicular distance। और centre of gravity है weight-weighted average position, जो gravity uniform होने पर centre of mass के बराबर है।
आख़िर में तीन types of equilibrium, इस हिसाब से कि छोटे disturbance पर centre of gravity कैसे हिलता है — stable के लिए ऊपर उठता, unstable के लिए गिरता, और neutral के लिए level रहता।

board_events.text: Take a light lever free to rotate about a fulcrum O; for no rotation, the net torque about O is zero.

board_events.latex: +F_1 d_1 - F_2 d_2 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; F_1 d_1 = F_2 d_2

board_events.text: Recipe step 1: draw a clean free-body diagram; weights act at the centre of gravity.
Step 2: apply force balance, the sum of horizontal forces and vertical forces each zero.
Step 3: take torques about a point where an unknown acts, so it drops out.
Step 4: solve, and a negative reaction just means you drew its direction backwards.

segments.text: Let us derive the principle of moments, then turn it into a recipe that cracks any rigid-body equilibrium problem.
The figure shows a light lever, free to rotate about a fulcrum O. A load force F one acts down at distance d one on one side, and an effort F two acts down at distance d two on the other.
Apply rotational equilibrium about the pivot. For the rod not to rotate, the net torque about O must vanish.

Write each torque with its sense. The load turns the rod one way, say anticlockwise and positive, the effort the other way, clockwise and negative. So plus F one d one minus F two d two is zero, which rearranges to F one d one equals F two d two, the principle of moments.
Now the recipe for any equilibrium problem. Step one: draw a clean free-body diagram, marking every external force at its point of application, and remember that weights act at the centre of gravity.
Step two: apply force balance, setting the sum of the horizontal forces to zero and the sum of the vertical forces to zero.
Step three, the art of it: take torques about a smartly chosen point, the point where an unknown force acts, because that force then has zero moment arm and drops out of the equation.
<whisper> Step four: solve the simultaneous equations, and sanity-check the signs. A negative reaction simply means you drew its direction backwards, so flip it and move on.
पहले principle of moments derive करते हैं, फिर उसे एक recipe में बदलते हैं जो किसी भी rigid-body equilibrium problem को तोड़ दे।
Figure एक light lever दिखाती है, जो fulcrum O के बारे में घूमने को स्वतंत्र है। एक load force F one एक तरफ़ distance d one पर नीचे act करता है, और एक effort F two दूसरी तरफ़ distance d two पर।
Pivot के बारे में rotational equilibrium लगाओ। Rod के न घूमने के लिए O के बारे में net torque ग़ायब होना चाहिए।

हर torque को उसके sense के साथ लिखो। Load rod को एक ओर घुमाता है, मान लो anticlockwise और positive, effort दूसरी ओर, clockwise और negative। तो plus F one d one minus F two d two बराबर zero, जो बनता है F one d one बराबर F two d two, principle of moments।
अब किसी भी equilibrium problem की recipe। Step one — एक साफ़ free-body diagram बनाओ, हर external force को उसके point of application पर mark करो, और याद रखो weights centre of gravity पर act करते हैं।
Step two — force balance लगाओ, horizontal forces का sum zero और vertical forces का sum zero रखते हुए।

Step three, इसकी असली कला — torques एक चतुराई से चुने point के बारे में लो, उस point पर जहाँ कोई unknown force act करता है, क्योंकि तब उस force का moment arm zero होता है और वह equation से निकल जाता है।
<whisper> Step four — simultaneous equations हल करो, और signs sanity-check करो। एक negative reaction बस यह मतलब है कि आपने उसकी direction उलटी खींची, तो पलट दो और आगे बढ़ो।

board_events.text: The stick is uniform and pivoted at its centre, so its own weight acts at the pivot: no torque.
Load $m_1 = 0.6$ kg at $d_1 = 0.20$ m; balancing $m_2 = 0.3$ kg at $d_2$.
The g cancels, so work directly with mass times distance.
Answer: the 0.3 kg mass hangs 40 cm from the pivot.

segments.text: A clean board-level balance. A uniform metre stick is pivoted at its centre. A zero point six kilogram mass hangs twenty centimetres from the pivot on one side. At what distance on the other side must a zero point three kilogram mass hang to balance it?
The figure sets it up: the pivot at the centre, the heavier mass close in on the left, and the lighter mass at an unknown distance on the right.
First a key simplification. Because the stick is uniform and pivoted at its centre, its own weight acts right at the pivot and produces no torque at all. We can ignore it.
Write the givens. The load is zero point six kilograms at zero point two zero metres, and the balancing mass is zero point three kilograms at the unknown distance d two.
Apply the principle of moments, mass one times distance one equals mass two times distance two. That is zero point six times zero point two zero equals zero point three times d two.
The left side is zero point one two, so d two is zero point one two over zero point three, which is zero point four zero metres.
Notice the g never appeared: it sits on both sides of the moment equation and cancels, so you work directly with mass times distance.
So the zero point three kilogram mass must hang forty centimetres from the pivot. Lighter mass, larger distance, exactly as balance demands.

एक साफ़ board-level balance। एक uniform metre stick अपने centre पर pivoted है। एक zero point six kilogram mass pivot से twenty centimetres दूर एक तरफ़ लटकी है। दूसरी तरफ़ किस distance पर एक zero point three kilogram mass लटके ताकि balance हो?
Figure इसे set करती है — centre पर pivot, बाईं ओर पास में भारी mass, और दाईं ओर एक unknown distance पर हलकी mass।
पहले एक अहम simplification। क्योंकि stick uniform है और centre पर pivoted, उसका अपना weight ठीक pivot पर act करता है और कोई torque नहीं बनाता। हम इसे नज़रअंदाज़ कर सकते हैं।
Givens लिखो। Load है zero point six kilograms, zero point two zero metres पर, और balancing mass है zero point three kilograms, unknown distance d two पर।
Principle of moments लगाओ, mass one गुणा distance one बराबर mass two गुणा distance two। यानी zero point six गुणा zero point two zero बराबर zero point three गुणा d two।
बायाँ हिस्सा है zero point one two, तो d two है zero point one two बटा zero point three, जो zero point four zero metres।
ध्यान दो g कभी आया ही नहीं — वह moment equation के दोनों तरफ़ बैठता है और cancel हो जाता है, तो आप सीधे mass गुणा distance से काम करते हो।
तो zero point three kilogram mass को pivot से forty centimetres दूर लटकना होगा। हलकी mass, बड़ी distance, ठीक जैसा balance माँगता है।

board_events.text: Trap: do not compute weights with g; it cancels. Use mass times distance.
$m_1 = 30$ kg at $d_1 = 1.5$ m; heavier $m_2 = 45$ kg at $d_2$.
The heavier child sits closer to the pivot.
Sanity: heavier and closer, lighter and farther, exactly what every real seesaw shows.

segments.text: A quick N E E T version of the same idea. A seesaw is balanced about its central pivot. A thirty-kilogram child sits one point five metres from the pivot. Where must a forty-five-kilogram child sit to balance it?
The figure previews the answer: the heavier child must sit closer to the pivot than the lighter one.
The trap here is procedural. Students start multiplying by g equals nine point eight to get weights. But g appears on both sides and cancels, so work directly with mass times distance.
Write the givens: thirty kilograms at one point five metres on one side, and the heavier forty-five kilograms at the unknown distance d two on the other.
Apply the principle of moments: thirty times one point five equals forty-five times d two.
The left side is forty-five, so d two is forty-five over forty-five, which is one point zero metre.
So the heavier forty-five-kilogram child sits one metre from the pivot, closer in than the lighter child.
<chuckle> And the sanity check is instant: the heavier child sits closer, the lighter one farther, exactly as intuition and every real seesaw demand.

उसी idea का एक झटपट N E E T version। एक seesaw अपने central pivot के बारे में balanced है। एक thirty-kilogram बच्चा pivot से one point five metres पर बैठा है। एक forty-five-kilogram बच्चे को कहाँ बैठना होगा ताकि balance हो?
Figure answer की झलक देती है — भारी बच्चे को हलके से pivot के ज़्यादा पास बैठना होगा।
यहाँ trap procedural है। Students g बराबर nine point eight से गुणा करके weights निकालने लगते हैं। पर g दोनों तरफ़ आता है और cancel हो जाता है, तो सीधे mass गुणा distance से काम करो।
Givens लिखो — एक तरफ़ thirty kilograms, one point five metres पर, और दूसरी तरफ़ भारी forty-five kilograms, unknown distance d two पर।
Principle of moments लगाओ — thirty गुणा one point five बराबर forty-five गुणा d two।
बायाँ हिस्सा है forty-five, तो d two है forty-five बटा forty-five, जो one point zero metre।
तो भारी forty-five-kilogram बच्चा pivot से one metre पर बैठता है, हलके बच्चे से ज़्यादा पास।
<chuckle> और sanity check तुरंत है — भारी बच्चा ज़्यादा पास, हलका ज़्यादा दूर, ठीक जैसा intuition और हर असली seesaw माँगते हैं।

board_events.text: Weight 200 N acts at the centre, $x=2$ m; support A at $x=0$, support B at $x=3$ m.
Take torques about A, so $N_A$ drops out (zero moment arm there).
Support B is nearer the weight, so it carries more; the sum returns 200 N.

segments.text: Now a J E E Main problem needing both equilibrium conditions together. A uniform beam four metres long weighs two hundred newtons and rests horizontally on two supports, one at the left end and one a metre from the right end. Find the reaction forces.
The figure lays it out: support A at the left end, support B at three metres, and the beam weight of two hundred newtons acting down at the centre, two metres along.
Set the geometry. The weight acts at the centre, at two metres; support A is at zero, support B is at three metres.
Step one, vertical force balance. The two upward reactions must add up to the weight, so N-A plus N-B equals two hundred newtons. Call it equation one.
Step two, the smart move: take torques about support A, so that the unknown reaction at A drops out, since it acts at A with zero moment arm.

The weight sits two metres from A, and support B is three metres from A. So N-B times three minus two hundred times two is zero, giving N-B as four hundred over three, about one hundred thirty-three point three newtons.
Back-substitute into equation one. N-A is two hundred minus one hundred thirty-three point three, which is sixty-six point seven newtons.
Check it physically: support B is closer to the centre of gravity, so it carries more of the load, and the two reactions add back to two hundred newtons. Both make sense.

अब एक J E E Main problem जिसे दोनों equilibrium conditions एक साथ चाहिए। एक uniform beam four metres लंबा है, weight two hundred newtons, और दो supports पर horizontally टिका है — एक बाएँ सिरे पर और एक दाएँ सिरे से एक metre दूर। Reaction forces निकालो।
Figure इसे बिछाती है — बाएँ सिरे पर support A, three metres पर support B, और beam का two hundred newtons weight centre पर, two metres पर, नीचे act करता।
Geometry तय करो। Weight centre पर, two metres पर act करता है; support A zero पर, support B three metres पर।
Step one — vertical force balance। दो upward reactions जुड़कर weight के बराबर हों, तो N-A plus N-B बराबर two hundred newtons। इसे equation one कहो।
Step two, चतुर चाल — torques support A के बारे में लो, ताकि A पर unknown reaction निकल जाए, क्योंकि वह A पर zero moment arm के साथ act करता है।

Weight A से two metres पर बैठा है, और support B, A से three metres पर। तो N-B गुणा three minus two hundred गुणा two बराबर zero, जो देता है N-B बराबर four hundred बटा three, लगभग one hundred thirty-three point three newtons।
Equation one में back-substitute करो। N-A है two hundred minus one hundred thirty-three point three, जो sixty-six point seven newtons।
इसे physically check करो — support B, centre of gravity के ज़्यादा पास है, तो ज़्यादा load उठाता है, और दोनों reactions जुड़कर वापस two hundred newtons बनते हैं। दोनों sense बनाते हैं।

board_events.text: Smooth wall gives only a horizontal $N_w$ at the top; rough floor gives $N_f$ and friction $f$.
Take torques about the foot, eliminating $N_f$ and $f$ (both act there).
Steeper ladder, smaller cot theta, less friction needed: stand it as upright as safe.

segments.text: A J E E Advanced classic. A uniform ladder of weight W and length L leans against a smooth vertical wall, making an angle theta with the rough floor. Find the minimum coefficient of friction at the floor needed to stop it slipping.

The figure marks every force. Because the wall is smooth, it gives only a horizontal normal at the top. The rough floor gives a vertical normal and a horizontal friction at the foot, and the weight acts at the midpoint.
So list them: the smooth wall gives only the horizontal normal N-w at the top; the rough floor gives the vertical normal N-f and the friction f at the bottom.
Force balance is quick. Horizontally, the friction equals the wall normal, f equals N-w. Vertically, the floor normal equals the weight, N-f equals W.
Now the key move: take torques about the foot of the ladder, which eliminates both N-f and f at once, since they act right there.

The weight acts at half the length, with a horizontal moment arm of half L cosine theta. The wall normal acts at the top, with a vertical moment arm of L sine theta. Setting the two moments equal gives N-w as half W cotangent theta.

Finally the friction condition. For no slipping, f is at most mu times N-f. Using the earlier relations, the minimum coefficient of friction is f over N-f, which is N-w over W, which is one half cotangent theta.
<curious> And the insight is practical: a steeper ladder means a larger theta, a smaller cotangent, and less friction needed. That is exactly why you stand a ladder as upright as it is safe to.

एक J E E Advanced classic। Weight W और length L की एक uniform ladder एक smooth vertical wall से टिकी है, rough floor के साथ theta angle बनाते हुए। Floor पर slipping रोकने के लिए न्यूनतम coefficient of friction निकालो।

Figure हर force mark करती है। Wall smooth है, इसलिए top पर सिर्फ़ एक horizontal normal देती है। Rough floor foot पर एक vertical normal और एक horizontal friction देता है, और weight midpoint पर act करता है।
तो इन्हें list करो — smooth wall top पर सिर्फ़ horizontal normal N-w देती है; rough floor bottom पर vertical normal N-f और friction f देता है।
Force balance झटपट है। Horizontally, friction बराबर wall normal, f बराबर N-w। Vertically, floor normal बराबर weight, N-f बराबर W।
अब key move — torques ladder के foot के बारे में लो, जो N-f और f, दोनों को एक साथ हटा देता है, क्योंकि वे वहीं act करते हैं।

Weight length के आधे पर act करता है, horizontal moment arm आधा L cosine theta के साथ। Wall normal top पर act करता है, vertical moment arm L sine theta के साथ। दोनों moments बराबर रखने पर N-w मिलता है आधा W cotangent theta।
आख़िर में friction condition। No slipping के लिए f ज़्यादा से ज़्यादा mu गुणा N-f। पहले वाले relations से, न्यूनतम coefficient of friction है f बटा N-f, जो N-w बटा W, जो one half cotangent theta।
<curious> और insight practical है — steeper ladder मतलब बड़ा theta, छोटा cotangent, और कम friction चाहिए। इसीलिए ladder को उतना upright खड़ा करते हैं जितना safe हो।

sections.title: Common pitfalls and pro-tips

board_events.text: Equilibrium traps that cost marks
1. Checking only one condition; a rigid body needs both $\sum F = 0$ and $\sum \tau = 0$.
Balancing forces but forgetting torques, or the reverse, is the number-one error.
2. Ignoring the weight of the support object; it acts at the centre of gravity.
3. Picking a poor pivot; choose the point where an unknown acts so it vanishes.
4. Confusing centre of mass with the point of support; balance needs support under the CG.
Pro-tip: take torques about the unwanted unknown; anticlockwise positive, and the side near the CG carries more.
That one choice turns a two-unknown problem into a single-step solution.

segments.text: Let us close equilibrium with the four traps and the pro-tip that collapses hard problems into one line.
Trap one, the number-one error: checking only one condition. A rigid body needs both the net force zero and the net torque zero.
Balancing the forces but forgetting the torques, or the reverse, sinks more equilibrium answers than anything else. Always write both.

Trap two: ignoring the weight of the support object itself. When a rod or plank has appreciable weight, that weight acts at its centre of gravity and must enter the torque equation, especially when the pivot is off-centre.
Trap three: picking a poor pivot. You may take torques about any point, so choose the point where an unknown force acts, and that force vanishes from the equation.
Trap four: confusing the centre of mass with the point of support. A body balances only when it is supported under its centre of gravity; support it elsewhere and gravity makes a toppling torque.

<whisper> And the pro-tip: for any find-the-reaction problem, take torques about the point where the unknown you care least about acts, so it disappears. Keep a sign convention, anticlockwise positive, and remember the side nearer the centre of gravity carries the larger load.
That single choice turns a messy two-unknown problem into a single-step solution, and the load-sharing check catches errors fast.
Equilibrium को उन चार traps और उस pro-tip के साथ बंद करते हैं जो कठिन problems को एक line में समेट देता है।
Trap one, नंबर-एक ग़लती — सिर्फ़ एक condition check करना। एक rigid body को दोनों चाहिए, net force zero और net torque zero।
Forces balance करके torques भूल जाना, या उलटा, बाक़ी किसी भी चीज़ से ज़्यादा equilibrium answers डुबोता है। हमेशा दोनों लिखो।

Trap two — support object के खुद के weight को नज़रअंदाज़ करना। जब किसी rod या plank का weight ठीक-ठाक हो, वह weight उसके centre of gravity पर act करता है और torque equation में आना चाहिए, ख़ासकर जब pivot off-centre हो।
Trap three — ख़राब pivot चुनना। आप torques किसी भी point के बारे में ले सकते हो, तो वह point चुनो जहाँ कोई unknown force act करता है, और वह force equation से ग़ायब हो जाता है।

Trap four — centre of mass को point of support से confuse करना। कोई body तभी balance करती है जब उसे centre of gravity के नीचे support किया जाए; कहीं और support करो तो gravity एक toppling torque बनाती है।

<whisper> और pro-tip — किसी भी find-the-reaction problem में, torques उस point के बारे में लो जहाँ वह unknown act करता है जिसकी आपको सबसे कम परवाह है, ताकि वह ग़ायब हो जाए। एक sign convention रखो, anticlockwise positive, और याद रखो centre of gravity के ज़्यादा पास वाला side बड़ा load उठाता है।
वही एक choice एक messy two-unknown problem को single-step solution में बदल देती है, और load-sharing check ग़लतियाँ जल्दी पकड़ता है।

sections.title: Moment of inertia: how hard it is to spin

board_events.text: Moment of inertia: how hard it is to spin

board_events.caption: Same mass; the ring resists spinning more than the disc
board_events.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 440 240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
<rect x="0" y="0" width="440" height="240" fill="#ffffff"/>
<text x="220" y="26" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#22303c">Where the mass sits decides the spin cost</text>
<circle cx="120" cy="120" r="60" fill="none" stroke="#2b6ca3" stroke-width="16"/>
<circle cx="120" cy="120" r="3" fill="#22303c"/>
<text x="120" y="205" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#2b6ca3">ring: all mass at the rim, M R squared</text>
<circle cx="320" cy="120" r="60" fill="#cfe0ea" stroke="#2b6ca3" stroke-width="2"/>
<circle cx="320" cy="120" r="3" fill="#22303c"/>
<text x="320" y="205" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#2f7d5a">disc: mass spread in, half M R squared</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Mass is resistance to a change in straight-line motion; moment of inertia is the same for spinning.
It depends not just on how much mass, but on where that mass sits relative to the axis.
Mass far from the axis is expensive to spin; mass near the axis is cheap.
Each particle contributes $m r^2$, so distance is squared: the outermost mass dominates.
A disc has half the moment of inertia of a ring of the same mass and radius.
Flywheels put mass at the rim for a large moment of inertia; a diver tucks in to spin fast.

segments.text: You already have a deep feel for mass: it is how hard it is to get something moving in a straight line. Moment of inertia is the exact same idea, but for spinning, how hard it is to get something rotating.
The figure shows the twist that makes it richer than mass. Two hoops of the same mass: one with all its metal at the rim, a ring, and one with the metal spread across the whole area, a disc.

Mass is the resistance to a change in linear motion. Push a loaded cart and an empty one with the same force, and the loaded one accelerates less. Moment of inertia is that resistance, but for angular motion.
And here is what makes it richer: moment of inertia depends not just on how much mass an object has, but on where that mass sits relative to the spin axis.
Mass far from the axis is expensive to spin; mass near the axis is cheap. You feel this whenever you choke up on a cricket bat and suddenly it whips around easily.

The reason is in the formula. Each particle contributes its mass times the square of its distance from the axis. Because the distance is squared, the outermost mass dominates, and a small shift of mass outward costs you dearly.
So spin a ring and a disc of the same mass and radius, and the disc has exactly half the moment of inertia of the ring. The ring keeps all its mass out at the rim, contributing the maximum.

<excited> Engineers exploit this. A flywheel puts most of its mass at the rim for a large moment of inertia, to resist changes in spin. Run it in reverse and a diver tucks into a tight ball to spin fast, then opens out to slow down.
Mass का आपको गहरा एहसास है — यह कितना मुश्किल है किसी चीज़ को सीधी line में हिलाना। Moment of inertia बिलकुल वही idea है, पर spinning के लिए, किसी चीज़ को घुमाना कितना मुश्किल है।
Figure वह twist दिखाती है जो इसे mass से ज़्यादा rich बनाता है। एक ही mass के दो hoops — एक जिसका सारा metal rim पर हो, ring, और एक जिसका metal पूरे area में फैला हो, disc।
Mass linear motion में बदलाव का विरोध है। एक भरी और एक ख़ाली cart को same force से push करो, भरी वाली कम accelerate करती है। Moment of inertia वही विरोध है, पर angular motion के लिए।
और यहाँ वह बात है जो इसे rich बनाती है — moment of inertia सिर्फ़ इस पर निर्भर नहीं कि कितनी mass है, बल्कि इस पर भी कि वह mass spin axis के relative कहाँ बैठी है।
Axis से दूर mass spin करने में महँगी है; axis के पास सस्ती। यह आप तब महसूस करते हो जब cricket bat पर हाथ ऊपर लाते हो और वह अचानक आसानी से घूमने लगती है।

वजह formula में है। हर particle अपनी mass गुणा axis से distance के square जितना contribute करता है। क्योंकि distance square होती है, सबसे बाहरी mass हावी रहती है, और mass का ज़रा सा बाहर खिसकना महँगा पड़ता है।
तो एक ही mass और radius के ring और disc को spin करो, disc का moment of inertia ring का ठीक आधा है। Ring अपनी सारी mass rim पर रखता है, maximum contribute करते हुए।

<excited> Engineers इसका फ़ायदा उठाते हैं। एक flywheel अपनी ज़्यादातर mass rim पर रखता है, बड़े moment of inertia के लिए, ताकि spin में बदलाव का विरोध करे। इसे उलटा चलाओ तो एक diver तेज़ घूमने के लिए एक tight गेंद में सिमटता है, फिर धीमा होने के लिए खुल जाता है।

board_events.text: Moment of inertia is always defined about a specific axis; there is no single value.
The $r$ in $m r^2$ is the perpendicular distance from the axis, not from a point or the CoM.
It depends on mass, its distribution, and the axis, but never on the angular velocity.
Radius of gyration $K$: the single distance at which all the mass would give the same $I$.
It is a compact way to describe how far the mass effectively sits from the axis.

segments.text: Before the formulas, three pieces of fine print that examiners test, and one clean new idea, the radius of gyration.

<curious> The figure shows that new idea. Imagine sweeping all the body mass to a single distance K from the axis, so that this point mass has the very same moment of inertia as the real, spread-out body.

Fine print one: the moment of inertia is always defined about a specific axis. The same body has different values about different axes, so there is no single the moment of inertia. Always ask about which axis first.
Fine print two: the r in mass times r squared is the perpendicular distance from the axis, not the distance from some point or from the centre of mass. Students lose marks by confusing these.

Fine print three: the moment of inertia depends only on the mass, its distribution, and the axis, never on the angular velocity. A body has the same moment of inertia whether spinning fast, slow, or sitting still.
Now the radius of gyration K. It is the single distance at which the whole mass could be concentrated to give exactly the same moment of inertia as the real body.
By definition, the moment of inertia equals the mass times K squared, so K is the square root of the moment of inertia over the mass.
It is a compact, single-number way to describe how far the mass effectively sits from the axis, and it makes several problems collapse to one line.
Formulas से पहले तीन fine print जो examiners test करते हैं, और एक साफ़ नया idea, radius of gyration।
<curious> Figure वह नया idea दिखाती है। कल्पना करो कि body की सारी mass को axis से एक single distance K पर समेट दो, ताकि इस point mass का moment of inertia असली, फैली हुई body के बराबर ही हो।

Fine print one — moment of inertia हमेशा एक specific axis के बारे में defined है। वही body अलग axes के बारे में अलग values रखती है, तो कोई एक the moment of inertia नहीं होता। पहले हमेशा पूछो किस axis के बारे में।
Fine print two — mass गुणा r square वाला r, axis से perpendicular distance है, किसी point या centre of mass से distance नहीं। Students इन्हें confuse करके marks गँवाते हैं।

Fine print three — moment of inertia सिर्फ़ mass, उसके distribution, और axis पर निर्भर करता है, कभी angular velocity पर नहीं। Body का moment of inertia वही रहता है, चाहे तेज़ घूमे, धीमे, या स्थिर बैठी हो।
अब radius of gyration K। यह वह single distance है जिस पर पूरी mass concentrated हो तो असली body के बिलकुल बराबर moment of inertia दे।
Definition से, moment of inertia बराबर mass गुणा K square, तो K है moment of inertia बटा mass का square root।
यह एक compact, single-number तरीक़ा है यह बताने का कि mass axis से असरदार तौर पर कितनी दूर बैठी है, और यह कई problems को एक line में समेट देता है।

segments.text: Here is the full moment-of-inertia toolkit: the definition, the two axis theorems, and the standard results you must have on instant recall.
The figure shows the two theorems side by side. The parallel-axis theorem shifts to any parallel axis, and the perpendicular-axis theorem works only for flat laminae.
The definition: the moment of inertia is the sum of each mass times the square of its perpendicular distance from the axis, or for a continuous body, the integral of r squared dee m.

The theorem of parallel axes, which works for any body: the moment of inertia equals the moment about a parallel axis through the centre of mass, plus the total mass times the square of the distance between the axes.
The theorem of perpendicular axes, which works only for flat, laminar bodies: the moment about the axis out of the plane equals the sum of the moments about two perpendicular in-plane axes.
Now the must-know values. A ring about its central axis is M R squared, a disc is half M R squared, a rod about its centre is M L squared over twelve, and about its end, M L squared over three.
<excited> For the round bodies: a solid sphere about a diameter is two fifths M R squared, a hollow shell is two thirds M R squared, and a solid cylinder about its own axis is half M R squared.
And keep the rule in your ear: the r is always the perpendicular distance from the axis, and the unit is kilogram metre squared.
यह रहा पूरा moment-of-inertia toolkit — definition, दो axis theorems, और वे standard results जो instant recall में होने चाहिए।
Figure दोनों theorems साथ-साथ दिखाती है। Parallel-axis theorem किसी भी parallel axis पर shift करता है, और perpendicular-axis theorem सिर्फ़ flat laminae के लिए चलता है।
Definition — moment of inertia है हर mass गुणा axis से उसकी perpendicular distance के square का sum, या continuous body के लिए, r square dee m का integral।
Theorem of parallel axes, जो किसी भी body के लिए चलता है — moment of inertia बराबर centre of mass से गुज़रते parallel axis के बारे में moment, plus total mass गुणा axes के बीच की distance का square।
Theorem of perpendicular axes, जो सिर्फ़ flat, laminar bodies के लिए चलता है — plane से बाहर axis के बारे में moment बराबर plane के अंदर दो perpendicular axes के बारे में moments का sum।
अब must-know values। Ring अपने central axis के बारे में M R square, disc आधा M R square, rod अपने centre के बारे में M L square बटा twelve, और अपने end के बारे में M L square बटा three।
<excited> गोल bodies के लिए — solid sphere एक diameter के बारे में two fifths M R square, hollow shell two thirds M R square, और solid cylinder अपने axis के बारे में आधा M R square।
और यह rule कान में रखो — r हमेशा axis से perpendicular distance है, और unit है kilogram metre square।

board_events.text: Perpendicular axis theorem: for a lamina, $r^2 = x^2 + y^2$ from the z-axis.

board_events.latex: I_z = \int (x^2 + y^2)\, dm = \int x^2\,dm + \int y^2\,dm = I_y + I_x

board_events.text: It needs every mass element in the plane, so it fails for spheres, cylinders, and cubes.
Laminar only: that single restriction is a favourite exam question.

segments.text: Two derivations in one section: the moment of inertia of a uniform rod, then a clean proof of the perpendicular-axis theorem.

The figure sets up the rod. Take a rod of mass M and length L lying along the x-axis, centred at the origin, with the rotation axis perpendicular to it through the centre. Take a small element of width dee x at distance x.
The rod is uniform, so its linear density is M over L, and the element mass dee m is that density times dee x. Each element sits at perpendicular distance x, so it contributes x squared dee m.

Integrate over the whole rod, from minus L over two to plus L over two. The integral of x squared gives L cubed over twelve, and with the density M over L in front, the moment of inertia is M L squared over twelve.
Now the perpendicular-axis theorem. For a flat lamina in the xy-plane, a mass element sits at distance r from the z-axis, where r squared is x squared plus y squared.

So the moment about the z-axis is the integral of x squared plus y squared, dee m, which splits into the integral of x squared plus the integral of y squared. Those are exactly the moments about the y-axis and the x-axis, so I-z equals I-x plus I-y.
Notice why the proof needs a lamina: it requires every mass element to lie in the plane. For a three-dimensional body that fails, so the theorem does not apply to spheres, cylinders, or cubes.
<whisper> That single word, laminar, is a favourite exam trap. Which shape can the perpendicular-axis theorem be applied to? Only a flat one.
एक ही section में दो derivations — पहले एक uniform rod का moment of inertia, फिर perpendicular-axis theorem का एक साफ़ proof।
Figure rod set करती है। Mass M और length L की एक rod लो जो x-axis पर हो, origin पर centred, rotation axis उसके perpendicular centre से गुज़रता। Distance x पर width dee x का एक छोटा element लो।
Rod uniform है, तो उसकी linear density है M बटा L, और element mass dee m है वह density गुणा dee x। हर element perpendicular distance x पर बैठता है, तो वह x square dee m contribute करता है।
पूरी rod पर integrate करो, minus L बटा two से plus L बटा two तक। x square का integral देता है L cube बटा twelve, और आगे density M बटा L के साथ, moment of inertia है M L square बटा twelve।
अब perpendicular-axis theorem। xy-plane में एक flat lamina के लिए, एक mass element z-axis से distance r पर बैठता है, जहाँ r square है x square plus y square।

तो z-axis के बारे में moment है x square plus y square, dee m का integral, जो टूटता है x square के integral plus y square के integral में। वे ठीक y-axis और x-axis के बारे में moments हैं, तो I-z बराबर I-x plus I-y।
ध्यान दो proof को lamina क्यों चाहिए — इसे हर mass element का plane में होना ज़रूरी है। एक three-dimensional body के लिए यह fail होता है, तो theorem spheres, cylinders या cubes पर लागू नहीं होता।
<whisper> वही एक शब्द, laminar, एक पसंदीदा exam trap है। Perpendicular-axis theorem किस shape पर लगाया जा सकता है? सिर्फ़ एक flat पर।

board_events.latex: I_{ring} = \int R^2\, dm = R^2\int dm = MR^2

board_events.text: A disc is nested rings; a ring at radius $r$, thickness $dr$, has mass $dm = \sigma\,2\pi r\, dr$.
Now verify the rod-end value with the parallel-axis theorem, shifting by $d = L/2$.
Chaining point mass to ring to disc to sphere is the master technique here.

segments.text: Two standard results fall out quickly, and they show how one derivation feeds the next.
Start with the ring, then build the disc from it, as in the figure: a disc is just nested rings, and we take a thin ring at radius r with thickness dee r.

The ring is the easy one. Every bit of a ring sits at the same distance R from the axis, so R comes straight out of the integral, leaving R squared times the total mass; the ring is M R squared. No calculus needed.
Now the disc, by stacking rings. A ring at radius r with thickness dee r has area two pi r dee r, so with the surface density sigma its mass is sigma times two pi r dee r.

Each ring contributes r squared dee m, so integrate from zero to R. The integral gives R to the fourth over four, and after tidying with the density, the disc is half M R squared. Notice the disc derivation used the ring result as its building block.
Now let us verify the rod-end value with the parallel-axis theorem, instead of re-integrating. The end axis is parallel to the central axis, a distance L over two away.

The moment about the end is the central value M L squared over twelve plus M times L over two squared. That is M L squared over twelve plus M L squared over four, which adds to M L squared over three, exactly the table value.

<excited> That chaining, point mass to ring to disc to sphere, and parallel-axis to shift anywhere, is the master technique for this entire subtopic. Learn to chain, and you rarely have to integrate from scratch.
दो standard results झटपट निकल आते हैं, और वे दिखाते हैं कि एक derivation अगली को कैसे खिलाती है।
Ring से शुरू करो, फिर उससे disc बनाओ, figure की तरह — एक disc बस nested rings है, और हम radius r पर thickness dee r का एक पतला ring लेते हैं।
Ring आसान है। Ring का हर हिस्सा axis से same distance R पर बैठता है, तो R सीधे integral से बाहर आ जाता है, बचता है R square गुणा total mass; ring है M R square। कोई calculus नहीं।
अब disc, rings को stack करके। Radius r पर thickness dee r के ring का area है two pi r dee r, तो surface density sigma के साथ उसकी mass है sigma गुणा two pi r dee r।

हर ring r square dee m contribute करता है, तो zero से R तक integrate करो। Integral देता है R की fourth power बटा four, और density के साथ साफ़ करने पर disc है आधा M R square। ध्यान दो disc derivation ने ring result को अपना building block बनाया।
अब rod-end value को parallel-axis theorem से verify करते हैं, फिर से integrate करने के बजाय। End axis, central axis के parallel है, L बटा two की distance पर।
End के बारे में moment है central value M L square बटा twelve plus M गुणा L बटा two का square। यानी M L square बटा twelve plus M L square बटा four, जो जुड़कर M L square बटा three, ठीक table value।

<excited> वही chaining, point mass से ring, disc, sphere, और parallel-axis से कहीं भी shift, इस पूरे subtopic की master technique है। Chain करना सीख लो, फिर आपको शायद ही कभी scratch से integrate करना पड़े।

board_events.text: Four masses on a square [CBSE Board]

board_events.caption: r is half the diagonal, so r squared is half a squared

board_events.text: Four masses of 2 kg each at the corners of a square of side 1 m; axis through the centre, perpendicular.
Use the perpendicular distance from the axis: half the diagonal, not half the side.
Answer: the moment of inertia is 4 kilogram metre squared.

segments.text: A board-level example that drills the definition. Four point masses of two kilograms each sit at the corners of a square of side one metre. Find the moment of inertia about an axis through the centre, perpendicular to the plane.
The figure shows the key distance. Each corner sits at the perpendicular distance equal to half the diagonal, not half the side.
Write the givens: two kilograms at each corner, side one metre, axis out of the plane through the centre.

The perpendicular distance of each corner from the centre is half the diagonal, which is a root two over two. So r squared is a squared over two, and with the side one metre, r squared is one half a square metre.
Apply the definition: the moment of inertia is the sum of each mass times r squared. All four masses are equidistant, so it is four times the mass times r squared.
Substitute: four times two times one half, which equals four kilogram metre squared.
The one thing to get right: use the perpendicular distance from the axis, which is half the diagonal, not half the side. That is the classic slip.
So the moment of inertia is four kilogram metre squared. Clean, once you use the right distance.

एक board-level example जो definition पक्की करती है। Two kilograms की चार point masses एक square के corners पर हैं, side one metre। Centre से गुज़रते, plane के perpendicular axis के बारे में moment of inertia निकालो।
Figure अहम distance दिखाती है। हर corner perpendicular distance पर बैठता है जो diagonal का आधा है, side का आधा नहीं।
Givens लिखो — हर corner पर two kilograms, side one metre, axis centre से plane के बाहर।
हर corner की centre से perpendicular distance है diagonal का आधा, जो a root two बटा two है। तो r square है a square बटा two, और side one metre के साथ, r square है one half square metre।
Definition लगाओ — moment of inertia है हर mass गुणा r square का sum। चारों masses equidistant हैं, तो यह four गुणा mass गुणा r square।
Substitute करो — four गुणा two गुणा one half, जो बराबर four kilogram metre square।
एक चीज़ सही करनी है — axis से perpendicular distance इस्तेमाल करो, जो diagonal का आधा है, side का आधा नहीं। यही classic slip है।
तो moment of inertia है four kilogram metre square। साफ़, जैसे ही आप सही distance इस्तेमाल करते हो।

sections.title: Worked example: radius of gyration, ring versus disc [NEET]

board_events.text: Radius of gyration, ring versus disc [NEET speed trap]

board_events.caption: Ring K equals R; disc K equals R over root two

<text x="220" y="26" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#22303c">Radius of gyration compared</text>
<circle cx="120" cy="120" r="55" fill="none" stroke="#2b6ca3" stroke-width="12"/>
<circle cx="120" cy="120" r="3" fill="#22303c"/>
<line x1="120" y1="120" x2="175" y2="120" stroke="#b3402f" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="120" y="200" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#2b6ca3">ring: K = R</text>
<circle cx="320" cy="120" r="55" fill="#cfe0ea" stroke="#2b6ca3" stroke-width="1.5"/>
<circle cx="320" cy="120" r="3" fill="#22303c"/>
<line x1="320" y1="120" x2="359" y2="120" stroke="#b3402f" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="320" y="200" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#2f7d5a">disc: K = R over root two</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Trap: no need for mass or integrals; the standard formula gives K, and mass cancels.
The ring has the larger radius of gyration.
Sanity: the ring keeps mass at the rim, so its effective distance is the full R.

segments.text: A quick N E E T trap on the radius of gyration. A ring and a disc have the same mass and the same radius. Find the radius of gyration of each about its central perpendicular axis, and say which is larger.
The figure previews both: the ring has radius of gyration equal to R, and the disc a bit less, R over root two.

The trap is to hunt for the mass or reach for integrals. But the radius of gyration is the square root of the moment of inertia over the mass, and the standard formulas make the mass cancel out entirely.
Write the definition: K is the square root of the moment of inertia over the mass.
For the ring, the moment of inertia is M R squared, so K is the square root of M R squared over M, which is simply R.
For the disc, the moment of inertia is half M R squared, so K is R over root two, about zero point seven zero seven R.
So the ring has the larger radius of gyration, and the mass never mattered.

<chuckle> The sanity check is neat: the ring keeps all its mass out at the rim, so its effective distance is the full R, while the disc spreads mass inward, pulling the effective distance below R. Physics and formula agree.
Radius of gyration पर एक झटपट N E E T trap। एक ring और एक disc की same mass और same radius है। हर एक का central perpendicular axis के बारे में radius of gyration निकालो, और बताओ कौन सा बड़ा है।
Figure दोनों की झलक देती है — ring का radius of gyration R के बराबर, और disc का ज़रा कम, R बटा root two।
Trap है mass ढूँढना या integrals की ओर जाना। पर radius of gyration है moment of inertia बटा mass का square root, और standard formulas mass को पूरी तरह cancel करा देते हैं।
Definition लिखो — K है moment of inertia बटा mass का square root।
Ring के लिए moment of inertia है M R square, तो K है M R square बटा M का square root, जो बस R।
Disc के लिए moment of inertia है आधा M R square, तो K है R बटा root two, लगभग zero point seven zero seven R।
तो ring का radius of gyration बड़ा है, और mass का कोई मतलब ही नहीं रहा।

<chuckle> Sanity check सुंदर है — ring अपनी सारी mass rim पर रखता है, तो उसकी effective distance पूरी R है, जबकि disc mass को अंदर फैलाता है, effective distance को R से नीचे खींचते हुए। Physics और formula मेल खाते हैं।

board_events.text: This needs both axis theorems in sequence: perpendicular first, then parallel.

board_events.latex: I_z = \tfrac12 MR^2 = I_x + I_y = 2I_d \;\Rightarrow\; I_d = \tfrac14 MR^2

board_events.text: A tangent in the plane is parallel to a diameter, a distance $d = R$ away.

board_events.latex: I_{tangent} = I_d + MR^2 = \tfrac14 MR^2 + MR^2 = \tfrac54 MR^2

board_events.text: Perpendicular axis gives the diameter value; parallel axis walks it to the tangent.
Skip either theorem and you are stuck: that is the hallmark of a JEE Main problem.

segments.text: A J E E Main problem that needs both axis theorems in sequence. Find the moment of inertia of a uniform disc of mass M and radius R about a tangent lying in the plane of the disc.
The figure shows the two steps. First the perpendicular-axis theorem gives the diameter value, then the parallel-axis theorem walks that out to the tangent.
So plan it as two moves. The perpendicular-axis theorem first, then the parallel-axis theorem.

About the central perpendicular axis, the moment is half M R squared. By symmetry the moment about any in-plane diameter is the same, so the perpendicular-axis theorem says half M R squared equals two times the diameter moment. Hence the diameter moment is a quarter M R squared.
Now the tangent. A tangent in the plane is parallel to a diameter, a distance R away.
Apply the parallel-axis theorem: the tangent moment is the diameter moment plus M R squared. That is a quarter M R squared plus M R squared, which is five quarters M R squared.
So the whole route is: perpendicular-axis theorem to get the diameter value, then parallel-axis theorem to reach the tangent.
<curious> Skip either theorem and you are stuck. Needing two theorems chained is the hallmark of a J E E Main moment-of-inertia question.
एक J E E Main problem जिसे दोनों axis theorems क्रम से चाहिए। Mass M और radius R की एक uniform disc का, disc के plane में पड़ी एक tangent के बारे में moment of inertia निकालो।
Figure दो steps दिखाती है। पहले perpendicular-axis theorem diameter value देता है, फिर parallel-axis theorem उसे tangent तक ले जाता है।
तो इसे दो moves में plan करो। पहले perpendicular-axis theorem, फिर parallel-axis theorem।

Central perpendicular axis के बारे में moment है आधा M R square। Symmetry से किसी भी in-plane diameter के बारे में moment same है, तो perpendicular-axis theorem कहता है आधा M R square बराबर two गुणा diameter moment। इसलिए diameter moment है एक-चौथाई M R square।
अब tangent। Plane में एक tangent, एक diameter के parallel है, R की distance पर।
Parallel-axis theorem लगाओ — tangent moment है diameter moment plus M R square। यानी एक-चौथाई M R square plus M R square, जो five quarters M R square।
तो पूरा रास्ता है — diameter value के लिए perpendicular-axis theorem, फिर tangent तक पहुँचने के लिए parallel-axis theorem।
<curious> किसी भी theorem को छोड़ो और अटक जाओगे। दो theorems को chain करना, एक J E E Main moment-of-inertia question की पहचान है।

<line x1="200" y1="100" x2="275" y2="100" stroke="#b3402f" stroke-width="1.5"/>
